---
title: "Probability distributions"
---

The extension provides 182 probability-evaluation functions: 13 parameterizations,
seven operations each, and scalar plus native `_array` forms, plus 13 explicitly
[seeded batch sampling functions](rng.qmd). Uniform, categorical and
permutation samplers have no probability functions and are described there. These return ordinary
PHP numbers and arrays. Distribution evaluation is separate from regression fitting;
`fit_poisson()` still fits a count model, while `dist_poisson_pmf()` evaluates a
specified Poisson distribution. [Descriptive statistics](descriptive.qmd) add ten
functions for supplied numeric slices. [Posterior-draw kernels](draw-numerics.qmd)
handle literal draw matrices.

## Families and parameterizations

Replace `{family}` in the operation names below with one of these names. PHP numeric
arguments accept integers or floats; binomial `size` specifically requires an integer.
All parameters must be finite and satisfy their domains.

| Family | Parameters in call order | Support and conventions |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `normal` | `mean = 0`, `sd = 1` | Real line; `sd > 0` |
| `t` | `df` | Standard Student t; `df > 0`, no location/scale arguments |
| `chisquare` | `df` | Nonnegative; `df > 0` |
| `f` | `df1`, `df2` | Nonnegative; numerator/denominator df both positive |
| `beta` | `alpha`, `beta` | `[0,1]`; both shape parameters positive |
| `gamma` | `shape`, `scale = 1` | Nonnegative; both positive; mean `shape * scale` |
| `exponential` | `rate = 1` | Nonnegative; positive rate; mean `1/rate` |
| `lognormal` | `meanlog = 0`, `sdlog = 1` | Positive; log X is Normal(meanlog, sdlog); `sdlog > 0` |
| `logistic` | `location = 0`, `scale = 1` | Real line; positive scale |
| `binomial` | `size`, `prob` | Integer successes `0..size`; size `0..2^53`, prob `[0,1]` |
| `poisson` | `lambda` | Nonnegative integer counts; lambda nonnegative |
| `nbinom` | `size`, `prob` | Failures before size-th success; real size > 0, prob `(0,1]` |
| `nbinom_mu` | `size`, `mu` | Same negative binomial; size > 0, mu ≥ 0; variance `mu + mu^2/size` |

Gamma's second parameter is **scale**, exponential's is **rate**. Negative-binomial
`size` is a positive real dispersion/shape parameter, not a binomial trial count.
The two NB forms are equivalent when `prob = size/(size + mu)`. Poisson lambda zero,
binomial size zero/prob zero/prob one, and NB prob one/mu zero represent point masses.
Parameter conversion in the mean-form NB avoids overflowing `size + mu`.

## Scalar and batch operations

| Operation | Scalar function | Definition |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Density | `dist_{family}_pdf(x, ...parameters)` | Continuous density f(x) |
| Log density | `dist_{family}_logpdf(x, ...parameters)` | Natural log of density |
| Mass | `dist_{family}_pmf(k, ...parameters)` | Discrete P(X = k) |
| Log mass | `dist_{family}_logpmf(k, ...parameters)` | Natural log of mass |
| CDF | `dist_{family}_cdf(x_or_k, ...parameters)` | P(X ≤ x) |
| Log CDF | `dist_{family}_logcdf(x_or_k, ...parameters)` | ln P(X ≤ x) |
| Survival | `dist_{family}_sf(x_or_k, ...parameters)` | P(X > x), evaluated directly |
| Log survival | `dist_{family}_logsf(x_or_k, ...parameters)` | ln P(X > x) |
| Quantile | `dist_{family}_quantile(p, ...parameters)` | Inverse CDF; p in `[0,1]` |

Continuous families expose pdf/logpdf; discrete families expose pmf/logpmf. Every
operation has an `_array` function taking a PHP array as its first argument and
the same parameters/defaults, for example:

```php
$probability = Phit\dist_normal_cdf(x: 1.96); // Approximately 0.975.
$tails = Phit\dist_t_sf_array(values: [1, 2, 3], df: 12);
$logMass = Phit\dist_poisson_logpmf_array(counts: [0, 2, 5], lambda: 3.2);
$interval = Phit\dist_gamma_quantile_array(probabilities: [.025, .975], shape: 2, scale: 3);
```

Scalar continuous evaluation uses argument `x`; discrete uses `k`. Batch continuous
evaluation uses `values`; discrete uses `counts`; all batch quantiles use
`probabilities`. Parameter names are part of the contract because PHP supports
named arguments. The generated `stubs/phit.php` lists every exact
signature. Loading the extension makes all functions available globally.

Batch evaluation constructs the distribution once, then streams input values
through the same core evaluation policy. Output is a packed list in input iteration
order; keys are not retained. Empty input returns `[]`, but parameters are still
validated. An invalid element rejects the entire call. No missing rows are dropped.
The [benchmarks](benchmarks/distributions.qmd) quantify when batching saves PHP
boundary overhead and when numerical evaluation dominates.

## Tails and likelihoods

Use survival functions for upper tails rather than subtracting a rounded CDF
from one. Use log functions directly rather than taking the log of a probability
that may already have underflowed.

```php
Phit\dist_normal_sf(10);     // About 7.62e-24; 1 - Phit\dist_normal_cdf(10) is zero.
Phit\dist_normal_logsf(40);  // About -804.61, even though the ordinary SF is zero.
$logLikelihood = array_sum(Phit\dist_poisson_logpmf_array([2, 5, 3, 0], lambda: 2.5));
```

A density is not a probability at a point and may exceed one. Sum log densities
or log masses for independent observations; likelihood underflow is avoided this
way. Log probabilities at impossible events are `-INF`. PHP JSON encoding with
`JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR` rejects nonfinite results; callers must choose their own
serialization policy rather than silently replacing numerical values.

The runnable `examples/distributions.php` demonstrates a two-sided t
test, a mean confidence interval, a Poisson likelihood, a central probability,
extreme upper tails and equivalent NB parameterizations. The sample data are
hypothetical and the computations illustrate the API.

## Boundaries and errors

Evaluation points may be ±INF, but NAN raises 1003. Null, numeric strings, booleans
and nested array elements are not numeric inputs; malformed batch elements raise
1001. Scalar argument-type failures follow Zend's runtime conventions. There is
no distribution `missing` option. Nonfinite parameters raise 1003; invalid domains
and quantile probabilities outside `[0,1]` raise 1001. Binomial size above `2^53`
raises 1007. A NAN numerical result raises 1006; it is not returned as a value.
Parameters so extreme that the incomplete beta or gamma cannot be evaluated also
raise 1006 promptly: a beta-type sum $a + b$ beyond the double range, a beta-type
parameter above $10^{300}$ evaluated within $10^{-300}$ of an end of the support, or
a gamma-type shape or point above $10^{300}$ (for example `dist_f_cdf(2, 3, PHP_FLOAT_MAX)`
or `dist_gamma_cdf(1e30, 1e30)`). Earlier builds could hang or panic on such input.

Outside support, density/mass is zero and log density/mass is `-INF`. Boundary
densities can be infinite, for example a beta shape below one at a support endpoint.
Discrete PMFs at non-integer counts are zero, while CDF/SF use the floor of the
evaluation point. SF always means strictly greater than that count.

Continuous quantile endpoints are the support bounds, including infinities. Discrete
quantiles return the smallest support value whose CDF reaches the requested
probability, using a documented `64 * EPSILON` relative comparison allowance on
the smaller tail to accommodate rounding at CDF steps. Endpoint p=0 follows the
conventional lower support bound; p=1 follows the upper support bound for ordinary
distributions. A point mass returns its actual mass location at p=1. This differs
from R/SciPy in some degenerate cases. Returned count quantiles are PHP floats;
precision is limited by binary64's exact integer range.

## Numerical implementation and dependency audit

The [raw statrs audit](verifications/distributions-audit.json) evaluates the saved
R cases with statrs 0.19, using log(CDF)/log(SF) because that crate has no log-tail
API. In these cases it loses small tails, has roughly `4.8e-4` relative binomial
CDF error at size one million, and suffers inaccurate extreme quantiles. Those
findings motivated a separate distribution module while retaining existing
estimator numerical paths.

| Families | Probability backend | Density and extreme-tail work |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Normal, lognormal | cdflib Cody normal tails | Split normal density; Mills-ratio log tails; safeguarded quantiles |
| Student t, F, beta | cdflib TOMS 708 incomplete beta | Stable log beta/gamma terms; log-scale incomplete-beta fraction |
| Gamma, chi-square | cdflib TOMS 654 incomplete gamma | Stable densities; log-scale gamma series/fraction |
| Binomial, negative binomial | cdflib incomplete beta | Loader-style saddle-point mass calculations; direct log tails |
| Poisson | cdflib incomplete gamma | Loader Poisson mass; log-scale gamma tails |
| Exponential, logistic | Closed-form Rust calculations | `expm1`, `log1p` and stable softplus formulas |

The runtime pins MIT-licensed `cdflib = 0.4.3`; GPL nmath ports were excluded by
the dependency audit. statrs remains the estimator dependency and a source of
special functions/seeds where appropriate. The implementation forms both tails
independently and uses custom log-scale expansions below `1e-280`. Continuous
quantiles use log-tail Newton steps protected by brackets. No R/Python/BLAS runtime
dependency is introduced. Numerical failure is explicit; this is not proof of
accuracy for every finite argument or arbitrarily extreme shape parameter.

## Reference evidence and release scope

[The executed comparison](verifications/distributions.qmd) records R, SciPy and
60-digit mpmath references, documented boundary differences and quantity-specific
tolerances. Scalar/batch identities and validation run in the offline release gate.
[Performance evidence](benchmarks/distributions.qmd) covers 1,000, 100,000 and one
million values, including peak process memory and regression preservation.

Random sampling uses explicitly seeded `dist_{family}_rng(n, seed, ...parameters)`
calls with local ChaCha20 state. The [sampling contract](rng.qmd) documents
reproducibility, validation and independent reference vectors.
[The readiness assessment](v0.2.qmd) records this implementation,
the estimator reuse experiment and remaining publication/platform gates.
